def sha_file(p):
    return hashlib.sha256(open(p, "rb").read()).hexdigest()


def rd(p):
    return open(p).read()


class Prose(str):
    """Always emitted as a folded block scalar."""


def P(text):
    return Prose(" ".join(text.split()))


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ YAML writer
def scalar_text(v):
    if v is None:
        return "null"
    if isinstance(v, bool):
        return "true" if v else "false"
    if isinstance(v, int):
        return str(v)
    if isinstance(v, float):        # measured seconds only; plain decimal form that YAML 1.1 reads back
        r = repr(v)
        assert re.fullmatch(r"-?\d+\.\d+", r), r
        return r
    if isinstance(v, str):
        if isinstance(v, Prose) or ": " in v or "\n" in v or v != v.strip() or v == "" \
                or v[0] in "'\"-{}[]>|*&!%@`#,?:":
            return None
        return "'" + v.replace("'", "''") + "'"
    raise TypeError("unsupported scalar %r" % (v,))


def folded(text, indent):
    body = " ".join(str(text).split())
    assert body == str(text), "folded value would change under whitespace folding: %r" % text
    width = max(40, 80 - indent)
    return [" " * indent + ln for ln in textwrap.wrap(body, width=width, break_long_words=False,
                                                       break_on_hyphens=False)]


def y_map(d, indent):
    out = []
    for k, v in d.items():
        out.extend(y_kv(k, v, indent))
    return out


def y_seq(lst, indent):
    out = []
    for item in lst:
        out.extend(y_item(item, indent))
    return out


def flow_ints(v):
    return "[" + ", ".join(str(x) for x in v) + "]"


def all_ints(v):
    return all(isinstance(x, int) and not isinstance(x, bool) for x in v)


def all_short_plain_str(v):
    return all(isinstance(x, str) and not isinstance(x, Prose) and scalar_text(x) is not None
               and len(x) < 20 for x in v)


YAML11_BOOLISH = {"y", "Y", "n", "N", "yes", "no", "on", "off", "true", "false"}


def y_kv(k, v, indent):
    pad = " " * indent
    if k in YAML11_BOOLISH:
        k = "'" + k + "'"           # keep keys such as N and n strings under every YAML 1.1 reader
    if isinstance(v, dict):
        return [f"{pad}{k}: {{}}"] if not v else [f"{pad}{k}:"] + y_map(v, indent + 2)
    if isinstance(v, list):
        if not v:
            return [f"{pad}{k}: []"]
        if all_ints(v) and sum(len(str(x)) + 2 for x in v) < 70:
            return [f"{pad}{k}: {flow_ints(v)}"]
        if all_short_plain_str(v) and sum(len(x) + 4 for x in v) < 70:
            return [f"{pad}{k}: [" + ", ".join(scalar_text(x) for x in v) + "]"]
        return [f"{pad}{k}:"] + y_seq(v, indent + 2)
    st = scalar_text(v)
    if st is None:
        return [f"{pad}{k}: >-"] + folded(v, indent + 2)
    return [f"{pad}{k}: {st}"]


def y_item(v, indent):
    pad = " " * indent
    if isinstance(v, dict):
        sub = y_map(v, indent + 2)
        return [pad + "- " + sub[0][indent + 2:]] + sub[1:]
    if isinstance(v, list):
        assert all_ints(v)
        return [pad + "- " + flow_ints(v)]
    st = scalar_text(v)
    if st is None:
        return [pad + "- >-"] + folded(v, indent + 2)
    return [pad + "- " + st]


def plain(obj):
    if isinstance(obj, dict):
        return {k: plain(v) for k, v in obj.items()}
    if isinstance(obj, list):
        return [plain(v) for v in obj]
    if isinstance(obj, str):
        return str(obj)
    return obj

    """Round-half-down of an exact terminating decimal at a tie (exact rational arithmetic)."""
    from decimal import Decimal
    from fractions import Fraction
    scaled = Fraction(Decimal(exact_str)) * 10000
    fl = scaled.numerator // scaled.denominator
    assert scaled - fl == Fraction(1, 2), exact_str
    return "%d.%04d" % (fl // 10000, fl % 10000)

def isprime(n):
    """
    Test if n is a prime number (True) or not (False). For n < 2^64 the
    answer is definitive; larger n values have a small probability of actually
    being pseudoprimes.

    Negative numbers (e.g. -2) are not considered prime.

    The first step is looking for trivial factors, which if found enables
    a quick return.  Next, if the sieve is large enough, use bisection search
    on the sieve.  For small numbers, a set of deterministic Miller-Rabin
    tests are performed with bases that are known to have no counterexamples
    in their range.  Finally if the number is larger than 2^64, a strong
    BPSW test is performed.  While this is a probable prime test and we
    believe counterexamples exist, there are no known counterexamples.

    Examples
    ========

    >>> from sympy.ntheory import isprime
    >>> isprime(13)
    True
    >>> isprime(15)
    False

    Notes
    =====

    This routine is intended only for integer input, not numerical
    expressions which may represent numbers. Floats are also
    rejected as input because they represent numbers of limited
    precision. While it is tempting to permit 7.0 to represent an
    integer there are errors that may "pass silently" if this is
    allowed:

    >>> from sympy import Float, S
    >>> int(1e3) == 1e3 == 10**3
    True
    >>> int(1e23) == 1e23
    True
    >>> int(1e23) == 10**23
    False

    >>> near_int = 1 + S(1)/10**19
    >>> near_int == int(near_int)
    False
    >>> n = Float(near_int, 10)  # truncated by precision
    >>> n % 1 == 0
    True
    >>> n = Float(near_int, 20)
    >>> n % 1 == 0
    False

    See Also
    ========

    sympy.ntheory.generate.primerange : Generates all primes in a given range
    sympy.functions.combinatorial.numbers.primepi : Return the number of primes less than or equal to n
    sympy.ntheory.generate.prime : Return the nth prime

    References
    ==========
    .. [1] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strong_pseudoprime
    .. [2] Robert Baillie, Samuel S. Wagstaff, Lucas Pseudoprimes,
           Math. Comp. Vol 35, Number 152 (1980), pp. 1391-1417,
           https://doi.org/10.1090%2FS0025-5718-1980-0583518-6
           http://mpqs.free.fr/LucasPseudoprimes.pdf
    .. [3] https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baillie-PSW_primality_test
    """

    # modulo tests benchmark faster than one or two primorial igcds for me.
    # The point here is just to speedily handle small numbers and many
    # composites.  Step 2 only requires that n <= 2 get handled here.
    if n in [2, 3, 5]:

       (n % 37) == 0 or (n % 41) == 0 or (n % 43) == 0 or (n % 47) == 0:
